title: Desert Ascetics
description: Antony, the Desert Fathers and Mothers, and why the Egyptian desert drew Christians out of the world

concepts.title: Antony and the Life That Made Him Famous
concepts.contentHtml:
Antony of Egypt (c. 251 to 356 CE) is the figure later Christians took as the first monk, though even his biography admits that older ascetics already lived on the edges of Egyptian villages. According to the Life of Antony, written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, soon after Antony's death (usually dated c. 356 to 362), Antony was the son of prosperous Christian farmers in Middle Egypt. Orphaned at about eighteen or twenty, he heard the Gospel read in church, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor" (Matthew 19:21). He gave away his land and placed his younger sister with a community of Christian virgins.

The Life traces stages of deepening withdrawal. First came an apprenticeship to an old ascetic near his village, then a stay in a tomb, then nearly twenty years shut inside an abandoned fort at Pispir near the Nile, and finally a retreat to the "Inner Mountain" near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of Saint Antony still stands. Throughout, demons assail him and he defeats them with prayer. The Life says he died aged about 105.

It's a text with an agenda. Athanasius presents Antony as an unlettered holy man loyal to the bishop's own anti-Arian theology. Seven letters attributed to Antony, defended as authentic by Samuel Rubenson (1990), suggest instead a man familiar with the philosophical theology of Origen. The Life was soon translated into Latin and became the model for saints' biographies. In his Confessions, Augustine recalls that hearing about it in 386 helped push him toward conversion.

concepts.title: Why the Desert Called
concepts.contentHtml:
By the late fourth century, monks and nuns had settled across Egypt. Hermits and small groups lived at Nitria, Kellia and Scetis (the Wadi al-Natrun) west of the Nile Delta, and large communal monasteries stood in Upper Egypt, organized from the 320s by Pachomius (c. 292 to 348). The Life of Antony boasts that "the desert was made a city by monks." Ancient visitors gave huge numbers, such as tens of thousands of monks and nuns in the single town of Oxyrhynchus, but historians treat such figures as rhetoric, not census data.

The sources explain the move in spiritual terms. Monks wanted to imitate Christ's fast in the wilderness, fight demons on their own ground, and prepare the soul for judgment. Historians add context. Persecution of Christians ended in the 310s, and with it the chance of martyrdom. The ascetic life came to be described as a daily martyrdom of the will, and some historians read the rush to the desert partly as a protest against a church that was becoming comfortable and powerful.

Social pressures may also have mattered. In Roman Egypt the Greek word anachōrēsis, "withdrawal," the root of "anchorite," already described peasants who fled their villages to escape taxes and compulsory public duties. Whether many monks were also fleeing such burdens is debated, since the evidence is indirect. Archaeology and papyri have softened the romantic picture in other ways. Much "desert" monasticism lay within a day's walk of the farmed Nile valley, monks sold baskets and rope in village markets, and some ascetics lived in or beside towns.

concepts.title: Sayings and Ascetic Rivalry
concepts.contentHtml:
The wisdom of the desert survives above all in the Apophthegmata Patrum, the Sayings of the Desert Fathers.1 These short anecdotes and replies circulated orally, largely in Coptic, and were written down in Greek, probably during the fifth century and probably in Palestine, where many Egyptian monks had moved. The alphabetical collection arranges sayings under the names of about 130 elders, while the systematic collection sorts them by theme, such as humility or discretion. Women appear as ammas, "mothers," among them Syncletica, Sarah and Theodora.

The sayings are terse. A brother asked Abba Moses for a word and was told, "Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything." Abba Arsenius heard a voice tell him, "Flee, be silent, pray." Abba Joseph, his raised fingers said to shine like ten lamps, told a visitor, "If you will, you can become all flame."

The sources also record ascetic rivalry, and mostly treat it as a danger. Palladius's Lausiac History (c. 420) says Macarius of Alexandria couldn't hear of any feat without trying to surpass it, and tells how he entered a Pachomian monastery in disguise and outdid its monks through all of Lent, until they complained to the abbot.2 Many sayings deflate such contests. In one, God reveals to Antony that a doctor in the city is his equal, because he gives his surplus to the poor and sings with the angels all day. Elders warn again and again that fasting without humility feeds pride, and that discretion, knowing the right measure, is the higher virtue.

title: Pillar Saints
description: Simeon Stylites, his imitators, and why Syrian villagers came to consult a man on a column

concepts.title: Simeon on the Pillar
concepts.contentHtml:
Simeon Stylites (c. 390 to 459 CE), named from Greek stylos, "pillar," was a shepherd's son from Sis, on the borders of Cilicia and Syria. He joined a monastery as a youth, but his austerities alarmed the community and he was asked to leave. He moved to the village of Telanissos (modern Deir Sem'an), about 30 km northwest of Aleppo, where he lived first enclosed in a hut and then chained within a small enclosure on a hilltop. As crowds of visitors grew, he climbed onto a column, probably around 420.

He remained on a series of ever taller pillars for the rest of his life, usually counted as about 37 years, though estimates range from about 35 to 42. The first column was perhaps 3 meters high; the last, by most accounts, was over 15 meters. Disciples climbed a ladder to bring food. Simeon stood, prayed, bowed and addressed crowds, exposed to Syrian summers and winters. He died on 2 September 459, and the patriarch of Antioch led his funeral.

Three early accounts survive and disagree in detail: the Religious History of Theodoret of Cyrrhus, a bishop who visited Simeon and wrote while he was still alive; a Greek Life attributed to a disciple named Antonius; and a longer Syriac Life dated 473. Theodoret knew he was describing something new and defends it against critics who found it absurd. He compares the pillar to the strange symbolic acts of Old Testament prophets, arguing that God sometimes uses startling sights to rouse the careless.

concepts.title: Pilgrims, Arbiters and Emperors
concepts.contentHtml:
Simeon's pillar drew visitors from across the late Roman world and beyond it. Theodoret lists Arabs, Persians, Armenians and Iberians (Georgians), with travelers from Spain, Gaul and Britain, and says that in Rome small images of Simeon were set up at the entrances of workshops for protection. Pilgrim tokens showing a stylite on his column, found far from Syria, confirm the reach of his cult.

Visitors came for healing and blessing, but also for judgment. In an influential 1971 article, the historian Peter Brown argued that Syrian holy men served villages as patrons and arbiters. Because a hermit stood outside kinship, property and local feuds, his verdict could settle a quarrel without either side losing face. The sources show Simeon giving audiences in the afternoon, resolving disputes, preaching against usury and swearing, and receiving whole groups of Arab tribesmen who renounced their old gods at the foot of the column.

His reach extended to the court. Emperor Theodosius II and the empress Eudocia valued his counsel, and when Emperor Leo I canvassed opinion on the Council of Chalcedon (451), Simeon wrote in its support. Later scholars, and Brown himself in later work, have qualified the model: holy men worked within church structures as well as outside them, and their perfect impartiality is partly an ideal of the hagiographers.

concepts.title: Daniel and the Stylite Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
Simeon had imitators. The best documented, Daniel the Stylite (c. 409 to 493), was born at Maratha near Samosata on the upper Euphrates and received Simeon's blessing as a young monk. He later settled at Anaplus on the European shore of the Bosporus, just north of Constantinople. After Simeon's death, and reportedly prompted by a vision of him, Daniel mounted a column there and stayed on pillars for about 33 years, as told in a Life written by a disciple soon after his death.

Living beside the capital made Daniel a political figure. Emperor Leo I visited him, became his patron, and brought foreign guests such as Gubazes, king of Lazica in the Caucasus. Officials climbed to ask advice. The Life says Daniel came down only once, during the usurpation of Basiliscus (475 to 476), to oppose the emperor's support for opponents of Chalcedon, and then returned to his pillar.

The practice spread unevenly. Simeon Stylites the Younger (521 to 592) took to a pillar near Antioch as a boy. In the West, Gregory of Tours tells of the deacon Wulfilaic, who stood on a column in the diocese of Trier until bishops told him that an obscure man could not rival Simeon and had the column broken up. In Syria, a great cross-shaped church, now called Qal'at Sim'an, was built around Simeon's pillar in the late fifth century, probably under Emperor Zeno. Pilgrims chipped the column away for relics until only a stump remained, and the site was reportedly damaged by a missile strike in 2016.

title: Enclosed Lives
description: Anchoresses enclosed beside English churches, Julian of Norwich, and the sealed retreats of Tibetan hermits

concepts.title: The Anchorhold and the Rite of Enclosure
concepts.contentHtml:
An anchorite (from Greek anachōrein, "to withdraw"), or in the female form an anchoress, was a Christian who vowed to live permanently enclosed in a small cell, usually built against the wall of a parish church. Unlike desert hermits, anchorites lived in the middle of towns and villages. In England the life flourished from the twelfth century until the Reformation: surviving records name about 780 anchorites at some 600 sites between 1100 and 1539, and the real total was surely higher. Women outnumbered men throughout, by as much as four to one in the thirteenth century.

An anchorhold was rarely more than about 4 meters square. One window, the "squint," looked into the church so that the recluse could see the altar and receive communion. Another opened onto a servant's room for food and necessities, and a curtained window let visitors seek advice. Nobody could simply decide to be enclosed. The bishop examined the candidate's vocation and made sure that a patron, relatives or an endowment would support the recluse for life, so that the parish would not be left with the burden.

The rite of enclosure borrowed from the liturgy for the dead. Versions varied, but in many the bishop recited prayers from the Office of the Dead, in some the candidate received the last rites, and the bishop might scatter earth before the door was shut and, in some cases, sealed or blocked. The message was that the anchorite had died to the world. The life largely ended in England when Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries between 1536 and 1539.

concepts.title: Ancrene Wisse and Julian of Norwich
concepts.contentHtml:
The best-known guide to the life is Ancrene Wisse ("Guide for Anchoresses"), written in the early thirteenth century in a West Midlands dialect of Middle English for three sisters of good family. Its author was a cleric: E. J. Dobson proposed Brian of Lingen, an Augustinian canon of Wigmore Abbey, while Bella Millett has argued for a Dominican friar. The book pairs an "outer rule" of practical arrangements with an "inner rule" about the heart, covering prayer, temptation, confession and love.

The tone is often moderate. The author tells the sisters to keep no animal but a cat, to avoid gossip at the window, and not to take up harsh penances, such as iron, hair shirts or scourging, without their confessor's permission. Excess is treated as a risk, not a goal.

Julian of Norwich (c. 1343 to after 1416) is the most famous English anchoress. On 8 May 1373, aged about thirty and so ill that she had received the last rites, she experienced sixteen visions, or "showings," centered on Christ's Passion. She recovered and wrote a Short Text and, over decades, a much longer version, together known as Revelations of Divine Love:1 the earliest surviving writings in English known to be by a woman. Her cell adjoined St Julian's church in Norwich, and "Julian" may be a name taken from it. Her birth name is unknown, as is whether she had been a nun or a widow. Wills left her money between 1394 and 1416, and the mystic Margery Kempe sought her advice around 1413. Her best-known line is "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."

concepts.title: Sealed Retreats in Tibet
concepts.contentHtml:
Enclosure has close parallels in Tibetan Buddhism, where a retreat is called tsam (written mtshams), literally "boundary." A practitioner seals a boundary around a hut, cave or room and stays inside it for a set period, usually with a helper who brings food. In the Kagyu and Nyingma schools the classic program is the three-year retreat, traditionally three years and three months, undertaken in purpose-built retreat centers; in those schools, completing it has often been the qualification for the title of lama. A few yogis vow lifelong retreat. The great exemplar of solitary practice is Milarepa (traditionally 1052 to 1135, though other dates are given), whose biographies describe years alone in mountain caves.

A modern case shows how such a life is supported. Tenzin Palmo, born Diane Perry in England in 1943, became a Tibetan Buddhist nun and lived from 1976 to 1988 in a cave in the Lahaul region of the Indian Himalayas, spending the last three years in strict retreat. Vicki Mackenzie's Cave in the Snow (1998) tells her story.

Comparison helps if the differences stay visible. Both traditions use enclosure as a controlled space for prayer or meditation, supported by a community that supplies food and receives blessing, advice or merit in return. Both require a teacher's or bishop's approval and warn against spiritual pride. But medieval English enclosure was normally for life and modeled on death, while most Tibetan retreats have a fixed term and end with a return to teaching. Western travelers' accounts of Tibetan hermits walled into dark cells, such as Alexandra David-Néel's, mix observation with romance and should be read with caution.

title: Bodies as Offerings
description: Medieval flagellant processions and the Jain vow of sallekhana, with the arguments each provoked

concepts.title: The Flagellants of 1260
concepts.contentHtml:
Public self-scourging as a mass movement first appears in Perugia in 1260. A hermit, Raniero Fasani, began preaching penance after reporting a vision, and the city government approved processions in which people of every class walked behind crosses and banners, stripped to the waist and striking their own backs with whips while singing and calling for mercy. That autumn the movement swept through central and northern Italy, and it crossed the Alps into southern Germany, Austria and Bohemia.

Historians point to several pressures. Italian cities were torn by the long war between Guelph and Ghibelline factions, famine and disease had struck in 1258 and 1259, and some followers of the abbot Joachim of Fiore (d. 1202) expected a new age of the Spirit to begin in 1260. How far ordinary penitents knew these prophecies is debated. Chroniclers stressed the movement's fruits: enemies reconciled, prisoners released, debts forgiven.

Authorities reacted in different ways. Many bishops and city councils welcomed the processions, while some rulers, wary of large uncontrolled crowds, closed their borders; the Ghibelline leader Oberto Pallavicino, then dominant in Milan, is reported to have set up gallows to keep them out. The mass phase faded within months, but it left a lasting institution: confraternities of disciplinati or battuti, lay brotherhoods that practiced penance privately and under written rules while also caring for the sick and burying the poor. Some survived for centuries, and penitential confraternities still hold processions in parts of Italy and Spain.

concepts.title: The Black Death Flagellants and the Church
concepts.contentHtml:
A second great wave came with the Black Death. In 1349 bands of flagellants, called Geissler in German, marched through Germany, the Low Countries and neighboring lands. Each pilgrimage lasted thirty-three and a half days, one day for each year of Christ's earthly life. Members needed their spouse's permission and enough money to pay their own way, and swore not to bathe, shave or sleep in a bed during the march. Twice a day they performed a public ritual of penance, which included reading a "Heavenly Letter" said to have been delivered by an angel, in which Christ threatened destruction unless people repented.

Their link to violence is disputed. In some towns, such as Frankfurt in July 1349, their arrival coincided with massacres of Jews, whom many Christians falsely blamed for poisoning wells. Norman Cohn's The Pursuit of the Millennium (1957) portrayed the flagellants as a radical, anticlerical and anti-Jewish movement. Later historians, notably Richard Kieckhefer, argued that most bands were far less radical and that many massacres took place before any flagellants arrived, while agreeing that processions could inflame crowds where they came.

The Church moved from tolerance to suppression. Pope Clement VI, who in 1348 had issued bulls denying that Jews caused the plague, condemned the flagellants in a bull of 20 October 1349 and ordered bishops to suppress them; theologians in Paris and the French king Philip VI also acted against them. The Church objected to mass penance led by self-appointed laymen outside its control.

concepts.title: Sallekhana: A Vow at the End of Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Jainism, which centers on ahimsa (non-harm), includes a practice outsiders often misread. Sallekhana, called santhara by many Śvetāmbara Jains, is a vow to let life end through the gradual renunciation of food and then drink, taken when death is already near. Classical texts such as the Ratnakaranda Śrāvakācāra, attributed to Samantabhadra, allow it only in specific circumstances: incurable illness, extreme old age, famine or unavoidable calamity, when normal religious life is no longer possible. It is undertaken openly, under a monk's or nun's guidance and with the family's knowledge.

Jains distinguish it sharply from suicide. Suicide, in Jain teaching, arises from passions such as despair or anger and often uses violent means; sallekhana is meant to be calm and dispassionate, a last act of detachment that loosens the bonds of karma. Memorial inscriptions at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka commemorate many such deaths from about the sixth century CE onward. Digambara tradition holds that the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta ended his life this way there, a claim that rests on much later sources. One estimate puts current numbers at about 240 a year in India.

In 2006 a lawyer, Nikhil Soni, filed a public interest petition in the Rajasthan High Court arguing that santhara was suicide. On 10 August 2015 the court agreed, holding that the practice was not an essential part of Jainism and was punishable as attempted suicide and abetment of suicide. Jains across India held silent protest marches, and on 31 August 2015 the Supreme Court of India stayed the ruling; the appeals then remained pending for years. Critics worry about pressure on the old and sick; defenders cite religious freedom.

title: Self-Mummified Buddhas and the Skoptsy
description: Japanese mountain ascetics who sought buddhahood in the body, and a Russian sect that saw the body as the enemy

concepts.title: Becoming a Buddha in This Body
concepts.contentHtml:
The Japanese word sokushinbutsu means "a buddha in this very body." It refers to a small number of preserved bodies of ascetics, seated in robes and venerated in temples, and to the long religious careers meant to produce them. The term echoes sokushin jōbutsu, "attaining buddhahood in this very body," a central teaching of Kūkai (774 to 835), founder of the Shingon school of esoteric Buddhism. Shingon tradition holds that Kūkai did not die but entered eternal meditation in his mausoleum on Mount Kōya, where monks still bring him meals each day.

Most sokushinbutsu are linked to Mount Yudono, one of the three sacred Dewa mountains in Yamagata Prefecture and a center of Shugendō, Japan's tradition of mountain asceticism, which blends esoteric Buddhism with the worship of local kami. The practitioners were usually not ordained temple monks but issei gyōnin, lifelong ascetics outside the monastic hierarchy. Over many years they kept mokujiki, "tree-eating," a diet that gave up cereals in favor of nuts, bark, roots and other wild foods, and they performed long seclusions on the mountain, such as a thousand-day retreat.

Temple traditions present these lives as offerings for others: prayers against the famines and epidemics that struck northeastern Japan repeatedly in the Edo period, and a vow to remain in the world until the coming of the future buddha Maitreya. The ascetics also depended on patrons and gave back. Tetsumonkai (d. 1829), now enshrined at Chūrenji, is remembered as much for building roads and traveling as far as Hokkaido as for his final austerities.

concepts.title: Survivors, Science and the Meiji Ban
concepts.contentHtml:
Many ascetics attempted the path, but few bodies survive: about seventeen or eighteen in Japan by most counts, eight of them in Yamagata Prefecture. The oldest known is Kōchi Hōin (d. 1363) at Saishōji in Niigata Prefecture. The Yamagata examples include Honmyōkai (d. 1683) at Honmyōji, Shinnyokai (d. 1783) at Dainichibō and Tetsumonkai at Chūrenji. They are venerated as living presences; Shinnyokai's robes are changed every twelve years.

Popular accounts describe a final step called dochū nyūjō, "entering meditation in the earth": the ascetic was sealed in a buried chamber with a bamboo breathing tube and a bell, and disciples dug him up three years and three months later. Evidence for this is thin, and much of it is later oral tradition. A scientific survey that began in 1959, led by Japanese researchers who went on to form the Japan Mummy Research Group, found that at least some bodies had been dried or otherwise treated by others after death, in one case by smoking. The popular claim that ascetics drank tea made from lacquer tree sap to preserve themselves appears in temple and tourist literature, but no Japanese example has been shown to be lacquered.

The early Meiji government, which promoted Shinto and separated it from Buddhism, ended the practice. An 1868 order banned the opening of graves, and live entombment came to be treated as assisting suicide; popular accounts give 1877 or 1879 for an outright ban, and the exact legal history is unclear. The last known case was Bukkai (1828 to 1903) of Niigata, whose followers could not legally exhume him. Researchers did so in 1961, and his remains are at Kannonji in Murakami.

concepts.title: The Skoptsy
concepts.contentHtml:
A very different discipline of the body appeared in Russia. The Skoptsy ("the castrated") emerged in the Oryol region in the late 1760s and early 1770s, splitting from the Khlysty, a secretive sect known for ecstatic worship and strict sexual abstinence; the first recorded investigation came in 1772. The Skoptsy went further. Teaching that sexual desire was the root of the Fall, they made castration of men, and comparable mutilation of some women, the mark of salvation, which they called "the seal." They cited Matthew 19:12 on those who made themselves eunuchs "for the kingdom of heaven's sake."

Their leader, Kondratii Selivanov (d. 1832), was revered by followers as a new Christ and, in some accounts, as Emperor Peter III in hiding. Flogged and exiled to Siberia in 1775, he later lived in St Petersburg under the protection of wealthy followers, until in 1820 he was confined to a monastery in Suzdal, where he died. Despite a secret and peasant origin, the sect came to include many merchants and townspeople and was known for thrift and commercial success.

The state treated the Skoptsy as dangerous, prosecuting, exiling and conscripting members. Their numbers are uncertain: an official count in 1866 found about 5,400, and later estimates ran far higher but are hard to verify. Some fled to Romania, where Skoptsy cab drivers became a familiar sight in Bucharest. Soviet trials in 1929 to 1931 effectively ended the movement. The historian Laura Engelstein's Castration and the Heavenly Kingdom (1999) reconstructs it from police files and members' own writings.

title: Old Believers and the Lykovs
description: The Russian schism of 1666, flight to Siberia, and the family geologists found in the taiga in 1978

concepts.title: The Schism of 1666
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1650s Patriarch Nikon of Moscow, backed by Tsar Alexis, set out to bring Russian worship into line with contemporary Greek practice. The changes look small from outside: making the sign of the cross with three fingers instead of two, singing "alleluia" three times instead of twice, spelling Jesus as Iisus rather than Isus, using five communion loaves instead of seven, and walking processions against the sun rather than with it. To many Russians they were not small. The old forms had been confirmed by a Moscow council in 1551, and Moscow saw itself as the guardian of true Orthodoxy after Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Changing the rite to match the Greeks implied that Russia's own saints had worshipped wrongly.

Nikon himself fell from favor, but the great Moscow councils of 1666 and 1667 upheld his reforms and anathematized those who rejected them. That split, the Raskol, created the Old Believers. Their most famous voice, Archpriest Avvakum, wrote an autobiography while imprisoned in the Arctic and was burned at the stake at Pustozersk in 1682. The Solovetsky Monastery on the White Sea held out against a government siege until 1676.

From the 1670s, some persecuted communities facing arrest chose collective death by fire rather than submit, believing the last days had come; estimates for the decades after 1667 run as high as 20,000 deaths, though such figures are uncertain. Later, Peter the Great made Old Believers pay a double tax. The Russian Orthodox Church lifted the anathemas in 1971.

concepts.title: The Lykovs: Into the Taiga
concepts.contentHtml:
Old Believers survived for centuries by moving away from the state, and many settled in Siberia and the Altai. Under Soviet rule, which attacked all religion, some fled again. In 1936, according to the family's own account, a Communist patrol shot and killed Karp Lykov's brother at the edge of their village. Karp, his wife Akulina and their children Savin and Natalia then vanished into the taiga of southern Siberia, in what is now the Republic of Khakassia. Two more children, Dmitry (born 1940) and Agafia (born 1944 or 1945), were born in the forest.

The family eventually settled in a log cabin near a tributary of the Abakan River, some 250 km from the nearest settlement. They had brought a spinning wheel, a few tools, icons and old liturgical books. They lived on potatoes, rye, pine nuts and what Dmitry could trap without a gun. Prayer structured their days, the children learned to read from the church books, and the family kept fasts and feasts by a calendar it maintained itself.

Isolation was dangerous. In 1961 a June frost destroyed their crops, and Akulina died of starvation, having given her share of food to her children. According to the journalist Vasily Peskov, the family recovered after a single rye grain sprouted and they carefully saved its seed. They knew nothing of the Second World War, although Karp noticed in the 1950s that some "stars" had begun to move quickly across the sky, and concluded that people must have invented something new.

concepts.title: Discovery, Agafia, and What Devotion Meant
concepts.contentHtml:
In the summer of 1978, a helicopter carrying geologists to survey for iron ore spotted a garden on a remote mountainside. A party led by the geologist Galina Pismenskaya found the family's cabin and an old man in a patched shirt made of sacking. The Lykovs were wary but gradually accepted visits and some gifts, above all salt, which they had lacked for decades. They refused most modern goods on religious grounds, though they took knives, tools and grain. Peskov's reports in Komsomolskaya Pravda from 1982 made them famous across the Soviet Union.

Contact may have had a cost. In the autumn of 1981, three of the four children died within weeks of one another: Savin and Natalia of kidney failure, probably linked to their meager diet, and Dmitry of pneumonia, after reportedly refusing to be flown to a hospital. Whether infections brought by visitors played a part is often suggested but cannot be proven. Karp died in February 1988.

Agafia stayed. She turned down offers to move to relatives in a village, reportedly tried life in an Old Believer convent for a time, and returned to the taiga, living with help from nature-reserve staff, occasional helpers, donors and the state. As of the mid-2020s she was reported to be still living there, in her eighties. She has explained her choice largely in religious terms, as loyalty to her parents' faith and way of life. For the Lykovs, devotion meant fidelity to a rite, a calendar and a family history of flight from persecution.
